`ops::compress::dot_unit` was four hand-written `std::arch` backends
(`dot_unit_{sse2,avx2,neon,scalar}`) behind `is_x86_feature_detected!`.
It is now
one generic kernel over
[`fearless_simd`](https://github.com/linebender/fearless_simd),
and that was **the last `unsafe` in EngramDB's own logic**.
(`engram-onnx` still
`dlopen`s the ONNX Runtime — nothing can do that safely.)

This required `[profile.release]` to move from `opt-level = "z"` to `3`.
The two are
one decision, not two: at `-Oz` nothing inlines, so the crate measured

*slower* than the intrinsics, and the intrinsics were the only way to
get vector
instructions into the binary at all.

process:

|---|---|---|---|
| scalar loop | 441.0 | 442.1 | 445.9 |
| intrinsics dispatch (was shipped) | 49.7 | 34.4 | 36.3 |
| **fearless_simd, 4 accumulators (ships)** | 184.9 | 33.7 | **34.3** |

| **`opt-level = 3` (ships)** | **117,390,224 (111.96 MiB)** | **136–138
ms** |

memories.title: compact on the query path, not inside `create`
memories.summary: Hanging the compaction trigger off the `create` tool was wrong, and the suite caught it: reindex_re_embeds_in_error_mode_despite_mismatch failed.
memories.content:
Hanging the compaction trigger off the `create` tool was wrong, and the
suite caught it: reindex_re_embeds_in_error_mode_despite_mismatch failed.

That test is named in CLAUDE.md as a known flake, but this was not it. It
failed in isolation as well as under parallelism, it passes on the base
commit, and bisecting the change to the create hook alone flipped it —
so the regression was mine.

The mechanism is real rather than a test artifact. `create` sets
embed_async: true and returns while a background ingest task is still
running, and that task stamps the embedding fingerprint on first embed
(retrieval/engine.rs). An extra await between the write and the tool's
return reorders the background stamp against a caller's own
set_embedding_fingerprint, so the real fingerprint can land last, the
mismatch disappears, and the gate that should fire does not. Any await
in that window does this; the trigger just happened to be the one that
introduced one.

So compaction moves to the `query` tool. Fragments are produced by
writes but only ever paid for by reads, which makes a query both where
the cost actually lands and a point with nothing else in flight. It also
keeps latency off the agent-facing write path, which it never should
have been on.

The CLI call site is unaffected: it runs in the dispatch before the
command, and CLI creates embed synchronously (embed_async: false), so
there is no background task to race.

memories.title: compact on fragment pressure, not only on a timer
memories.summary: Query latency tracks LanceDB fragment count rather than row count: at a fixed 400 rows, 100 uncompacted creates take the index projection from 5.9 ms to 42.0 ms.
memories.content:
Query latency tracks LanceDB fragment count rather than row count: at a
fixed 400 rows, 100 uncompacted creates take the index projection from
5.9 ms to 42.0 ms. optimize() already existed and ops::maintenance
already called it, but only behind the full pass's 6-hour throttle — so
a write-heavy session served several-fold slower queries for the rest of
the window.

The full pass keeps that throttle, because it does expensive work (a
registry sweep and a store health scan). Compaction now gets its own,
much cheaper trigger in ops::maintenance::auto_compact: stat one marker
file, and only if a short throttle has expired open the store, read
fragment metadata via the new LanceIndex::fragmentation (LanceDB's
stats(), which reads fragment metadata and never row data), and run
optimize() when small_fragments exceeds the threshold.

Two [maintenance] knobs, both defaulted conservatively:
  compaction_fragment_threshold = 32   (0 disables, keeping the old
                                        purely time-based behaviour)
  compaction_min_interval_secs = 120

The throttle deliberately gates the *probe*, not just the compaction.
Stamping the marker only on the compacting path would leave a
below-threshold store paying a store open and a LanceDB stats call on
every single invocation — the probe is the expensive half of the common
case. Stamping up-front also stops a slow or failing compaction from
becoming a hot retry loop across concurrent invocations. Regression test
pins this.

Wired into both front-ends: the CLI dispatch beside auto_maintain, so
every ordinary command is an opportunity, and the MCP server's create
tool plus maintain_main_project — an MCP session is long-lived and
writes throughout, so startup-only would have missed the case that
matters most.

memories.summary: Adds examples/query_stage_profile.rs and the measurements it produced, taken to price a proposed daemon-side memory cache. The cache question turned out to be secondary.
memories.content:
Adds examples/query_stage_profile.rs and the measurements it produced,
taken to price a proposed daemon-side memory cache. The cache question
turned out to be secondary.

Query cost is set by LanceDB fragment count, not row count. At a fixed
400 rows, 100 uncompacted creates take list_for_filtering from 5.9 to
42.0 ms (7.1x) and vector_search from 3.5 to 15.7 ms (4.4x) — a full
query going ~21 ms -> ~102 ms with no new data. Every LanceDB-touching
stage degrades; embed and get_batch, which touch no LanceDB, stay flat.
An earlier uncompacted 300-row store measured list_for_filtering at
141 ms, 24x its compacted figure.

optimize() already exists and ops::maintenance already calls it, with a
comment anticipating exactly this. But it is throttled to
[maintenance].interval_secs (default 6 hours) and skipped for hooks, so a
write-heavy session sits at ~5x degraded latency for the rest of the
window. Triggering compaction on fragment count as well as elapsed time
is a small change to an existing pass that recovers the whole 4-7x.

Two corrections to what this review previously assumed:

- The file-read path is not hot. get_batch(30) is 2.2 ms (11% of a
  healthy query) with a ~0.9 ms floor from two dirent scans and ~0.02 ms
  per additional memory, and it is 1.3x immune to fragmentation. Caching
  parsed .md memories — the obvious "stop reading disk every time" fix —
  targets the cheap stage. The projection is what to cache.
- The embedding forward pass is 3.8 ms, ~19%. The 211 ms model load is
  the expensive part and the daemon already amortizes it.

15.7 -> 53.3 ms fragmented). It is there for ranking correctness and has

memories.title: measure recall against embedding dimension (R7)
memories.summary: R2 reported that 4-bit quantization costs 12-25% of top-1 results, but that figure is specific to d=384 and the document did not say so.
memories.content:
R2 reported that 4-bit quantization costs 12-25% of top-1 results, but
that figure is specific to d=384 and the document did not say so.

Sweeping d in {384, 768, 1024, 1536} at 4-bit with TQ+ shows top-1
agreement against exact cosine going 0.80 -> 0.97 -> 1.00 -> 1.00 at
n=2000. TurboQuant's coordinate-distribution assumption is asymptotic in
d, so 384 is close to its worst case among realistic embedding widths.
The accuracy objection is therefore an artefact of our narrow embedding,
not a property of the algorithm.

Nothing else moves, though, and the lever costs more than it returns:

- Break-even n stays ~311-339 vectors at every width, because the fixed
  per-index overhead scales linearly with d (451 KB -> 1666 KB) at the
  same rate the data does. R1 is untouched.
- The storage case turns circular: d=1536 at 4-bit is ~780 B/vector
  against today's d=384 f32 at 1536 B/vector, a net 1.97x — quadrupling
  the width to compress it 8x and landing at half.
- No 1536-dim local model exists. The provider table tops out at 1024
  (mxbai-embed-large-v1), which embedding-model-alternatives.md finding 5
  already re-confirmed as a "don't switch". 1536 means an API model,
  against the offline design the ONNX stack exists for.
- It slows the dominant term. Warm embed is 5.70 ms against a ~100-500 us
  scan; a wider model costs multiples of that, and turbovec's own scan
  goes 4x slower (124 -> 518 us).

So the dimension lever works and is not worth pulling for this reason. If
a wider model is ever adopted on retrieval-quality grounds, R2 stops
being a blocker and turbovec earns a fresh look.

memories.title: measure the per-project harvest search cost
memories.summary: Fills in the one number the evaluation was missing, and it changes R6's recommendation rather than confirming it.
memories.content:
Fills in the one number the evaluation was missing, and it changes R6's
recommendation rather than confirming it.

A single project's conversation search costs 5.55 ms at *4 rows* — where
the k-NN is free by construction — so that figure is entirely fixed
overhead, and it is 17x turbovec's whole load-and-query (316 us).

But the cheap fix this document originally proposed only recovers a fifth
of it. Reusing the Connection and Table handles lands at 4.45 ms against
cold's 5.55 ms, so the three open_table calls are ~1.1 ms and the
remaining ~4.45 ms is the two DataFusion query plans themselves — ~2.2 ms
per vector query, per project, per search, independent of row count.

So the ordering is: cache the Table handle (small, helps every caller),
then ask whether the two per-column queries can be avoided — noting Lance
k-NNs one vector column per query, so collapsing them is a question for
LanceDB rather than a known fix, and skipping summary_vec when a project
has no curated summaries is the safe half of it. A flat file is third,
and still needs a row store for the 15 scalar columns every hit renders,
which brings the per-project open back.

Also corrects the caveat list: R6 is now measured, against a synthetic
table matching the conversations shape rather than a real store.

memories.summary: Measures the TurboQuant quantized index (turbovec 1.0.0) against both vector paths — memory/chunk vectors and the harvest conversation index — and records why it is not worth adopting.
memories.content:
Measures the TurboQuant quantized index (turbovec 1.0.0) against both
vector paths — memory/chunk vectors and the harvest conversation index —
and records why it is not worth adopting.

The headline results are all about scale mismatch. turbovec's benchmarks
are at n=100K, d=1536/3072; EngramDB runs d=384 at 10^2-10^4 vectors:

- A fixed 248 KB (2-bit) / 451 KB (4-bit) per-index overhead at d=384
  means break-even against raw f32 is ~339 vectors at 4-bit. Below that
  the "16x compression" crate is strictly larger than the data.
- 4-bit costs 12-25% of top-1 results against exact cosine, degrading as
  n grows. 2-bit is unusable. The reranker cannot recover a memory that
  never entered the shortlist.
- The in-kernel allowlist — the one feature that looked like a genuine
  fit — is sublinear (1% selectivity buys ~2x, not ~100x), is slower than
  no filter when everything is allowed, and returns Err(UnknownId) for
  any absent id. Our restrict lists legitimately carry ids with
  has_embedding = false. Both paths already push down real prefilters.

Also records the architectural friction (sync API into an async layer, a
writer lock on a deliberately lock-free read path, u64 ids vs our UUID
strings, no place for a .tvim blob in a migration that rebuilds from the
.md files) and the one path where the shape is still plausible: the
per-project LanceDB opens in machine-wide harvest search, where caching
the Table handle is the cheaper fix to try first.

crate with its own [workspace] table so turbovec never enters the

memories.content:
## Summary

CLI output had no golden coverage — `docs/contributors/testing.md` said
so outright ("Snapshot/golden tests: There are none"), and the renderer
tests could assert nothing stronger than "it did not panic" because
`OutputFormatter` called `println!` directly. This adds **325 snapshots
across two tiers**, covering every subcommand, every output format, and
both success and error outcomes.

Test count goes from 1825 to 2150; no production behavior changes except
the two bug fixes below.

## The two tiers

The suite is split by *what it can prove*, not by convenience:

- **Tier 1 — the renderers** (`crates/engram-cli/src/output.rs::tests`,
snapshots in `crates/engram-cli/tests/snapshots/renderer/`). Every
`OutputFormatter::print_*` × `pretty`/`json`/`plain`, driven in-process
from fixtures with pinned ids and pinned clocks. **Nothing is redacted**
— a reviewer reads the actual bytes instead of a field of placeholders.
This is where layout lives.
- **Tier 2 — the binary** (`crates/engram-cli/tests/cli/snapshot/`).
Spawns real `engramdb` and snapshots command line + exit code + stdout +
stderr. Exit codes, stream routing through a real pipe, and clap's
exit-2 parse errors are unreachable in-process (`run` returns
`anyhow::Result<()>`; the `Error: …` text comes from `Termination` in
`main.rs`), so they can only be pinned here.

Most tier-2 cases use the default format only. The exceptions are the
*renderer-thin* commands — `config`, `stats`, `daemon`, `review`,
`doctor` — which print with bare `println!` rather than through
`OutputFormatter`, so tier 1 can't see them and tier 2 sweeps all three
formats instead.

memories.summary: Removes several quadratic per-memory loops in the storage and ops layers, adds explicit SIMD to the compress-path dot product, and narrows the cross-project stats scan.
memories.content:
Removes several quadratic per-memory loops in the storage and ops
layers, adds explicit SIMD to the compress-path dot product, and narrows
the cross-project stats scan. Every change is backed by a Criterion
benchmark committed alongside it; a few candidate optimizations were
measured, found not to pay, and are documented as rejected rather than
shipped.

## Batching

- **`MemoryStore::update_batch_with`** — one lock, one batched read, one
index upsert, one manifest refresh for a set of mutations. `update_with`
in a loop measured 28 ms/memory at n=16 rising to 60 ms/memory at n=128
(quadratic). Wired into `task complete` and `consolidate_cluster_apply`.
`write_updated_locked` is split into file and index halves so the batch
path *reuses* the durability ordering rather than copying it.
- **`get` → `get_batch`** in `close_superseded_windows`, both
`compress_apply` loops, `consolidate_cluster_apply` and the pretty `gc`
branch. Measured 3.8x at n=16 rising to 24x at n=128.
- **Chunk reads** — `export_chunks_batch` / `upsert_chunks_batch`
replace per-memory chunk queries on the reindex and consolidation paths.

memories.title: make a failed daemon start discoverable instead of silent
memories.summary: ## The bug An auto-spawned daemon is **detached** — it outlives the process that started it — and it was spawned with `stderr(Stdio::null())`.
memories.content:
## The bug

An auto-spawned daemon is **detached** — it outlives the process that
started it — and it was spawned with `stderr(Stdio::null())`. Every
reason it could fail to start (bind error, missing ONNX runtime, panic
on first model load) was written to a stream that discarded it.

Callers fall back to in-process models by design, and that part is
correct. The defect is that the failure left **no trace anywhere**, so a
user whose daemon never starts has nothing to look at.

## One correction to the framing

There is **no PID file** to go stale. Coordination is the socket itself,
and stale-socket reclaim already works: bind a per-pid temp path,
`rename` atomically over the target, serialized by an advisory `flock`.

So the self-heal was never missing. What was missing is that **when the
self-heal can't succeed, nothing says so.**

## Four changes

**1. The spawned daemon's stderr goes to a log** —
`<global_data_dir>/logs/daemon.log` instead of `/dev/null`.

That directory is a sibling of `projects/` and `global/`. I checked all
eight consumers of `global_data_dir()`: every one descends into
`projects/` or `global/` specifically, and the only enumerating scan
(doctor's orphan-project sweep) is scoped to `projects/`. A new sibling
is inert.

Opened append-with-cap: past 1 MB it truncates on open. A crash-looping
daemon writes the same failure forever, and an unbounded diagnostic file
would be its own bug.

**2. A hand-run `engramdb daemon run` keeps its terminal.** Diverting to
a file you'd then have to `tail` is worse than useless when you're
watching. The rule is a pure function of TTY-ness so it's testable; the
redirect uses `dup2` rather than reconfiguring `tracing`, because the

memories.title: keep fuzz/Cargo.lock from drifting off the root workspace
memories.summary: Removes the cause of the drift #84 repaired. ## Why it drifted `fuzz/` declares its own `[workspace]` — the cargo-fuzz layout, which keeps libfuzzer and its nightly sanitizer flags out of ordinary bui
memories.content:
Removes the cause of the drift #84 repaired.

## Why it drifted

`fuzz/` declares its own `[workspace]` — the cargo-fuzz layout, which
keeps libfuzzer and its nightly sanitizer flags out of ordinary builds.
That also makes it invisible to dependabot's `directory: "/"` entry.

So `fuzz/Cargo.lock` went untouched from **#56** while the root's moved
with every batch, until the two had drifted far enough that `cargo check
--locked` **failed inside `fuzz/` on a clean checkout** and any
resolution there rewrote ~3200 lines.

## Why workspace inheritance can't fix it

Worth stating, since it's the obvious first idea. Two independent
blockers, both verified:

1. **A crate owning a workspace cannot inherit from an outer one.**

memories.content:
Fixes #64.

## Not a crash — a build failure

The auto-filed issue says "crash inputs are in the artifact" and gives a
`cargo fuzz run <target> <crash-file>` repro line. Neither applies: the
fuzzer never started.

```
error[E0277]: `(u8, f64, f64, i64, _, _, Option<String>, ...)`
              doesn't implement `std::fmt::Debug`
  --> fuzz_targets/composite_score.rs:23:1
```

`fuzz_target!` formats its input with `{:?}` so it can print the failing
case, and std implements `Debug` only up to **arity 12**. The target's
input tuple had grown to 15. (Verified empirically: a 12-tuple compiles,
a 13-tuple gives exactly this `E0277`.)

## It is a regression, not a target that never worked

Worth correcting, since it changes what this means: the target was
created with **11 fields** in #43 — comfortably under the limit — and
built and ran fine. **#60** (epistemic classes) added four fields,
pushing it to 15 and silently breaking the build.

So the composite-score finite-score invariant *was* being exercised, and
has gone unexercised from #60 until now. This restores real coverage
rather than enabling it for the first time.

That invariant matters: ranking sorts on `final_score` with
`partial_cmp(..).unwrap()`, which panics on `NaN`, and `criticality` is
parsed from on-disk memory files with a plain `f64::parse` — so a file
can carry `NaN`/`inf`.

## The fix

Replace the tuple with a `#[derive(Debug, Arbitrary)] struct
ScoreInput`. A struct has no arity ceiling, so fields can be added
freely from here. The named fields also remove the hazard of silently
misaligning a 15-way positional destructuring.

Adds `arbitrary` with its `derive` feature. Version 1.4.2 was already in
the lockfile via `libfuzzer-sys`, so `derive_arbitrary` is the only
genuinely new crate — the lockfile diff

## Bug 1 — an empty summary acquires the title

A memory with a **title** and an **empty summary** silently gained its
title as the summary on re-parse:

```
written:   **Summary:**
rewritten: **Summary:** Weird --- "quoted" title
```

**Root cause** — a two-sided asymmetry:

1. The writer emits `**Summary:** ` whenever a title is set, even when
the summary is empty, leaving a bare prefix.
2. `extract_bold_field` rejects that line via `if !val.is_empty()` and
returns `None`.
3. The reader resolved `None` with `.unwrap_or(h1)` — and for a titled
memory the H1 holds the **title**.

**The adversarial input was a red herring.** The `---` and quotes play
no part; reducing the crash input shows the trigger is *any titled
memory whose body has no unindented H1*:

| body shape | 1st parse | 2nd parse | idempotent |
|---|---|---|---|
| no h1 / indented h1 / empty body | `""` | `"T"` | ❌ |
| unindented h1 | `"Other"` | `"Other"` | ✅ |

**Fix:** drop the H1 fallback on the titled branch only. The untitled
branch still reads its summary from the H1 — there the H1 legitimately
*is* the summary, per the format doc-comment (`# <summary>`) — and a
control test pins that.

**User impact:** the fabricated summary is embedded for semantic search,
so the memory matched on its title text twice, distorting retrieval.

## Summary

Reranking ships **on** for the first time, running a uint8 cross-encoder
at `top_n = 10` for an estimated ~150 ms/query — roughly 5× cheaper than
`enabled = true` would have cost at the previous default of 50.

Four commits, each independently reviewable.

## The measurement

Three labeled corpora. Two were built for this PR: a 45-query/144-pair
"hard" set (101 memories) and a 10-query/46-pair set (75 memories), each
graded by **three independent labelers working blind to every ranking**,
with inter-annotator agreement of 0.44–0.66 Jaccard. The third is the
existing 48-query synthetic set.

Ungated reranking **never loses** — positive or neutral on every metric
of every corpus:

| corpus | baseline nDCG@10 | reranked | notable |
|---|---|---|---|
| hard frontend (101 mem) | 0.660 | **0.684** | R@5 +0.077 |
| easy eclinics (75 mem) | 0.884 | 0.884 | MRR 0.950 → **1.000** |
| graded synthetic (60 mem) | 0.941 | **0.942** | R@5 +0.017 |

`top_n = 10` is the measured knee, and is **both cheaper and better**
than the old default of 50 (nDCG 0.684 vs 0.690 at a fifth of the
cross-encoder calls). `top_n = 5` drops *below* baseline, so the window
must not shrink further.

The quantized model is a strict improvement over the fp32 export it
replaces: **1.55× faster inference at equal quality** (nDCG 0.945 vs
0.946), 36.5 MB instead of 144 MB, warm load at parity (172 ms vs 159
ms).

`ops::build_engine_without_providers` wires no reranker regardless of
config, so `PreToolUse` / `SessionStart` / `UserPromptSubmit` — which
fire on every Read/Write/Edit — never pay cross-encoder latency. That
guarantee was incidental; `hook_engine_never_reranks` now pins it.

memories.summary: ## Summary Started as a model-stack evaluation and turned into a correctness fix.
memories.content:
## Summary

Started as a model-stack evaluation and turned into a correctness fix.
The headline finding: **the prebuilt ONNX Runtime we shipped executes
quantized models incorrectly on AVX-512/AMX hosts.** Under CPU load the
same text embedded to 44 distinct vectors in 60 trials, with cosine
below zero — and those vectors get persisted, so the corruption is
durable.

It is the *build*, not the version or the model. Microsoft's own 1.24.2
is bit-reproducible on identical files. So EngramDB stops carrying a
runtime entirely: the binary resolves one from the user's system at
startup, and no artifact we publish contains a copy in any form.

(`onnxruntime#6004`), MiniLM-L12 for embeddings,
`jina-reranker-v1-turbo-en` for reranking, with a per-model cost matrix

(default) and `bundled-onnxruntime` (an opt-in escape hatch for hermetic
builds — nothing we release uses it). Release archives contain the
binary and nothing else, on every target; packages declare a dependency
on the platform's runtime.

panics on a missing dylib and the release profile is `panic = "abort"`,
so shipping load-dynamic naively would turn "user hasn't installed

memories.content:
## Summary

Adds a memory tier **between** a single project and the machine-wide
global store: a memory relevant to a *specific set* of projects (a
monorepo family / related repos on one machine), including the ability
to share a **single** memory to an **arbitrary subset** of projects.

Design:
[`docs/plans/2026-07-20-multi-project-memories.md`](docs/plans/2026-07-20-multi-project-memories.md)
(accepted-design panel + owner-confirmed decisions).

**Model:** *named group stores* (`C`) + a per-memory `audience` filter
(`B`'s precision, without content-less stubs). A shared memory is a
first-class, embedded record in exactly one store (a named group store,
or the everyone/global store) — real content ⇒ real embedding ⇒ native
semantic recall, and every within-store mechanism (`supersedes`,
challenge/NLI, gc/decay, single `flock`, fingerprint) keeps working
unmodified. No duplication, no dangling pointers. Global is unified as
the built-in "everyone" group.

## What's included

**Schema & migration**
- Nullable `audience` field on `Memory` (TOML frontmatter) + one LanceDB
column; `manifest::CURRENT_SCHEMA_VERSION` bumped `0.3.0 → 0.4.0`;
existing stores backfill on open via the standard reindex-from-`.md`
path (no re-embed). A non-member project with no group memories behaves
byte-for-byte as before.

**Group stores & membership**

## Summary

A benchmarked overhaul of what EngramDB embeds, driven by a controlled
offline study of chunking, model choice, and embed-text composition
(full report: `docs/contributors/embedding-analysis.md`).

**Headline finding:** the biggest retrieval-quality lever isn't the
model or chunk size — it's that title and tags never reached the
embedding. Fixing that (as a separate metadata vector per memory) lifts
MRR@10 from 0.75 → 0.89 and P@1 from 0.67 → 0.85 on the default model,
replicated across all four models tested. Model swaps (BGE-small, nomic)
were refuted: no gain above the noise floor at 5–7× the CPU latency.

## What changed

### Production
- **Metadata vector** (`embeddings.metadata_vector`, default **on**):
each memory embeds a dedicated `"{title}. {summary}. tags: …"` row plus
content-only chunks, replacing the single `"{summary} {content}"` text.
Max-score aggregation, the freshness guard, and `has_embedding` are
unchanged; `false` restores the legacy composition.
- **Composition tracking**: `EmbeddingFingerprint` gains an optional

migration). A new `CompositionMismatch` status flows through the

--embeddings-only`" signal instead of a silent mixed-composition index.

max_words/4)` words is rebalanced with its predecessor (midpoint
re-split) instead of becoming its own noisy vector — and, unlike naive
appending, never pushes text past the provider's silent token
truncation.

## Summary

Every memory now carries an **epistemic class** — `fact`, `observation`,
or `decision` — orthogonal to its memory type, answering *what kind of
claim is this* so the system can decay, rank, dispute, and retire
knowledge appropriately. Design and rollout follow the in-repo spec
(`docs/plans/2026-07-19-epistemic-memory-spec.md`, decisions D1–D7) and
its implementation/test plans.

Backward compatibility is anchored on two rules: the type→class default
mapping is frozen (`context`/`convention`/`relationship`/`hazard` →
fact, `debug` → observation, `decision`/`intent`/`preference` →
decision), and the file writer emits the new fields **only when
off-diagonal** — a memory that never uses them round-trips
byte-identical (golden tests enforce it). Existing stores migrate with a
single schema bump (0.2.0 → 0.3.0, reindex-on-open, vectors preserved).

**Bi-temporal validity (§2.4)** — memories are *invalidated*, not
deleted: `supersedes` on create/update, `resolve` with `action:

all close a validity window (`invalidated_at` + `superseded_by`).

windows by default; `--include-invalidated` shows history;

memories.summary: ## Summary The review feature (`ops::review`, the CLI `review` command, and the MCP `review` tool) only ever surfaced memories explicitly flagged `NeedsReview`/`Challenged`.
memories.content:
## Summary

The review feature (`ops::review`, the CLI `review` command, and the MCP
`review` tool) only ever surfaced memories explicitly flagged
`NeedsReview`/`Challenged`. Long-lived stores accumulate **active**
memories nobody has revisited, and nothing prompted agents or users to
re-verify them, so knowledge silently goes stale.

This PR adds a **recency-based review trigger**: active memories that
haven't been touched in longer than a configurable window are suggested
for review, and the MCP surface proactively hints at doing so. It is a
*review nudge, not a TTL* — nothing is ever deleted or hidden.

The design follows agent-memory best practice: use timestamp metadata to
detect aging knowledge, but — because plain TTL is *indifferent to
utility* — rank stale memories by **criticality** rather than blindly
expiring them.

## What changed

- **Config** — new `[review].recency_days` (default `90`, validated
`1..=3650`, mirroring `stats.retention_days`).
- **`ops::review`** — `ReviewParams::stale_after_days` unions age-stale
*active* memories with the flagged set. `updated_at` is the recency
anchor because every edit and every `resolve` (keep/update) bumps it, so
routinely-touched memories never go stale. Results stay ranked by
criticality. A `0`-day or overflowing window is treated as "off" rather
than "all".
- **`ops::count_recency_stale`** — cheap, index-only helper (no `.md`
loads) for the count shown in the hint.
- **MCP `review` tool** — new `stale_after_days` param; when omitted it
defaults to the project's `recency_days`, and the response echoes the
effective window as `recency_days`.
- **MCP `memory-session-end` prompt** — reports how many active memories
are past the window so an agent can offer to revisit them (the primary
"surface a hint" path).

memories.content:
## Summary

Adds an end-to-end benchmark suite under
`benches/memory-search-benchmark/` that drives **real `engramdb serve`
MCP sessions** (stdio JSON-RPC) through the `query`/`get` (search) and
`create` (save) tools, measuring latency, memory, and concurrency for
**in-process** vs the **shared embedding daemon**.

Along the way it fixes a real bug: the **MCP server ignored
`ENGRAMDB_IN_PROCESS`**, so an early version of the benchmark routed
*both* execution modes through the daemon (a no-op comparison).

## The fix — MCP server honors `ENGRAMDB_IN_PROCESS`

The CLI had an `--in-process` / `ENGRAMDB_IN_PROCESS` flag ladder; the
MCP server had no equivalent and always used the daemon when
`daemon.enabled`.

- New shared helper `engram_types::in_process_override()` (truthy
`1`/`true`/`yes`/`on`), the single source of truth for the env var.
- `engram-mcp`'s `daemon_path_enabled` now returns
`config.daemon.enabled && !in_process_override()`, so the env var
disables **both** provider routing and the daemon heartbeat (no stray
daemon spawn) — mirroring the CLI.
- `engram-cli` refactored onto the same helper (removes a duplicated
inline parse).

Respects the inward-only module DAG (helper lives in the `engram-types`
leaf; both front-ends depend on it). Validated at runtime:
`ENGRAMDB_IN_PROCESS=1` → serve RSS ~391 MB (model in-process), no
daemon spawned; unset → serve ~40 MB + daemon ~378 MB.

## Benchmark suite

memories.title: CLI opt-in, heartbeat self-heal, session-aware idle
memories.summary: ## Summary Makes the shared embedding daemon a first-class, self-healing, session-aware resource instead of an MCP-only, fire-and-forget process. Three user-facing goals: 1.
memories.content:
## Summary

Makes the shared embedding daemon a first-class, self-healing,
session-aware resource instead of an MCP-only, fire-and-forget process.
Three user-facing goals:

1. **CLI uses the daemon** (opt-in, connect-only) — model-needing CLI
ops route through a running daemon instead of paying the ~240 ms ONNX
cold-load every invocation. Overridable with `--in-process` /
`ENGRAMDB_IN_PROCESS` / `[daemon].use_for_cli = false`; spawning stays
opt-in via `--spawn-daemon`.
2. **MCP self-heals** — a session detects a dead/replaced daemon and
re-spawns it, instead of silently degrading to in-process for the rest
of its life (the old `OnceCell` cached a `None` failure for the process
lifetime).
3. **Session-aware idle** — the daemon stays resident while any agent
session is connected and reaps only after the last one ends.

Plus heartbeat observability: `daemon status` now shows `pings: N (last
Xs ago)`.

Design & plan:
`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-06-03-daemon-lifecycle-design.md`,
`docs/superpowers/plans/2026-06-03-daemon-lifecycle.md`.

## How it works

- **Backbone** — one `ops::resolve_providers` shared by CLI and MCP,
backed by a re-resolvable `ops::DaemonCell` (replaces the permanent
`OnceCell`). The cell health-checks a cached handle on each resolve and
re-spawns a dead daemon, rate-limited to one spawn per `idle/3` window
(only *failed* spawns consume the window).
- **Heartbeat (Design B)** — a per-MCP-process background task resolves
via the cell every `max(30s, idle/3)`. Each resolve sends a `Ping`,
which refreshes the daemon's idle clock (keep-alive) and re-spawns it if
dead (self-heal). No persistent connection, no concurrency rework; the
daemon's existing idle watchdog is unchanged.
- **Protocol v2 → v3** — `DaemonStatus` gains `ping_count` +
`last_ping_secs_ago

memories.summary: ## Summary The Test job installs nextest with `cargo install cargo-nextest --locked`, which **compiles nextest from source** (release profile).

## Summary

The Test job installs nextest with `cargo install cargo-nextest
--locked`, which **compiles nextest from source** (release profile). On
a cache miss that step takes **~7 min** (observed 6m52s in a prior run)
and consumes build disk. `Swatinem/rust-cache` only masks this on a
cache *hit* — evictions (7-day idle, 10 GB repo-cache limit), new
branches, and cache-key changes all pay the full compile.

## Change

Install the **prebuilt** nextest binary via `taiki-e/install-action` —
nextest's recommended GitHub Actions install method:

```diff
       - name: Install nextest
-        run: cargo install cargo-nextest --locked
+        uses: taiki-e/install-action@v2
+        with:
+          tool: nextest
```

Downloads in seconds, every run, regardless of cache state. Pinned to
`@v2` to match the repo's existing action-pinning style
(`actions/checkout@v4`, `Swatinem/rust-cache@v2`,
`softprops/action-gh-release@v2`). Also frees rust-cache from carrying
the nextest binary.

Only the Test job is affected (Check & Lint doesn't use nextest).

## Validation

- `ci.yml` validates as YAML.
- The real confirmation is the Test job's "Install nextest" step time on
this PR's CI run dropping from minutes to seconds.

memories.title: resolve the engramdb bin via workspace default-members
memories.summary: ## Summary The release workflow is **broken on `master`** after the workspace split (#44).
memories.content:
## Summary

The release workflow is **broken on `master`** after the workspace split
(#44). The `engramdb` binary now lives in the `engram-cli` crate, while
the workspace-root package is the `engramdb` core lib, so a root build
fails:

```
$ cargo build --release --bin engramdb
error: no bin target named `engramdb` in default-run packages
help: available bin in `engram-cli` package:
    engramdb
```

This breaks both release jobs (`build-arm`, `build-intel`).

## Fix

Treat the workspace as a whole via `default-members` rather than
hard-coding the package in the workflow:

```toml
[workspace]
members = ["crates/*"]
default-members = [".", "crates/*"]
```

This makes bare root commands (`cargo build`/`test`/`clippy`/`run`) act
on every member — matching the repo's `--workspace`-everywhere
convention — and lets `cargo build --bin engramdb` resolve the binary
without `-p`. The release steps go back to the plain `cargo build
--release --bin engramdb`. Hand-pick a single crate with `-p` when you
want a faster, narrower build.

Packaging is unchanged: workspace members share the root `target/`, so
the artifact is still at `target/release/engramdb`.

## Why default-members over `-p engram-cli`

`-p` would also fix the workflow, but `default-members` additionally
removes a footgun: a bare `cargo test`/`clippy` (forgetting
`--workspace`) previously covered only the root core lib and silently
skipped the other crates. With the whole workspace as the default set,
bare commands do the right thing.

## Validation

- Reproduced the failure on `master`; confirmed the fix resolves it.
- `cargo build --bin engramdb` resolves and builds at the workspace
root; `cargo metadata` lists all 8 crates as default members.
- `release.yml` validates as YAML. `ci.yml` (uses explicit
`--workspace`)

Splits the former single-crate `engramdb` monolith into a **layered

The codebase was one crate doing everything (CLI, MCP server, embedding

memories.title: The layered design
memories.summary: The arrows are dependency direction. The layers above only depend on the layers below.
memories.content:
The arrows are dependency direction. The layers above only depend on the layers below.

The layers are real Cargo workspace crates: `engram-cli` and `engram-mcp` are
front-ends over the `engramdb` core lib (the root crate, `src/`), and the core
re-exports the extracted leaf crates (`engram-storage`, `engram-models`,
`engram-types`, `engram-onnx`) under their historical module paths
(`engramdb::storage`, `::embeddings`, `::types`, …). See
[code-organization.md](./code-organization.md) for the full crate map.

memories.title: The one big rule: ops is shared
memories.summary: The CLI and the MCP server are **two surfaces over the same operations**. Every memory operation lives in `src/ops/<name>.rs` with typed input/output structs.
memories.content:
The CLI and the MCP server are **two surfaces over the same operations**. Every memory operation lives in `src/ops/<name>.rs` with typed input/output structs. The CLI parses Clap args, builds the typed params, calls ops, formats the result via `OutputFormatter`. The MCP server parses MCP tool arguments, builds the typed params, calls ops, serializes the result as MCP tool output.

Concretely, for a single operation like `create`:

If you put logic in `crates/engram-cli/src/commands/add.rs` instead of `src/ops/create.rs`, the MCP tool will diverge from the CLI command. This has happened — don't repeat it. The single-ops-impl rule prevents silent skew.

memories.title: One table, not two
memories.summary: There is no separate metadata DB. The LanceDB table has both the columns we filter on (`type`, `tags`, `criticality`, `physical`, `logical`, `status`, …) and the vector column.
memories.content: There is no separate metadata DB. The LanceDB table has both the columns we filter on (`type`, `tags`, `criticality`, `physical`, `logical`, `status`, …) and the vector column. Filtering happens at the LanceDB layer; vector search is the same table with an ANN query. This is why `IndexFilterable` / `VectorMatch` / `IndexSummary` types are in `crates/engram-storage/src/lance_index.rs` — they're the API into that one table.

memories.title: Concurrency model
memories.summary: Mutating ops (`create`, `update`, `delete`, `reindex`, `upsert_chunks`, `delete_chunks`) take a **per-project** advisory `flock(2)` from `crates/engram-storage/src/write_lock.rs`.
memories.content:
Mutating ops (`create`, `update`, `delete`, `reindex`, `upsert_chunks`, `delete_chunks`) take a **per-project** advisory `flock(2)` from `crates/engram-storage/src/write_lock.rs`. This serializes concurrent writes across processes — multiple Claude Code sessions can safely write to the same store.

Reads are lock-free. LanceDB's MVCC handles concurrent readers.

File writes use atomic temp-then-rename to prevent partial reads — even a hard kill mid-write leaves either the old file or the new file, never half of each.

memories.title: Worktree routing
memories.summary: When you run a memory command inside a git worktree, the CLI dispatch (`engram_cli::run`) checks `storage::worktree::resolve_project_root` first. If the cwd is a linked worktree, it: 1.
memories.content:
When you run a memory command inside a git worktree, the CLI dispatch (`engram_cli::run`) checks `storage::worktree::resolve_project_root` first. If the cwd is a linked worktree, it:

1. Locates the main worktree's project.
2. Ensures the main project is initialized (init it if needed).
3. Registers the current worktree as a sub-project linked to the main.
4. Consolidates any memories the user accidentally wrote to a stray worktree-local `.engramdb/`.
5. Routes the op to the main project.

Five commands are exempt: `init`, `serve`, `completions`, `setup`, `daemon`. They have their own working-directory semantics; auto-routing would silently target the wrong place.

memories.title: The model-fingerprint invariant
memories.summary: Every store records a fingerprint of the embedding model it was built with: `model_id()` + `dimensions`, stored in `.engramdb/manifest.toml`.
memories.content: Every store records a fingerprint of the embedding model it was built with: `model_id()` + `dimensions`, stored in `.engramdb/manifest.toml`. The fingerprint table and the provider resolver **both derive from one map**, `provider_specs(provider_str)` in `src/ops/mod.rs`. Adding a new provider requires updating exactly one place — see [`.claude/CLAUDE.md`](../../.claude/CLAUDE.md) for the silent-vector-corruption footgun this prevents.

memories.title: Provider caching
memories.summary: `ProviderCache` in `src/ops/mod.rs` keys loaded model bundles by `provider_cache_key = backend|provider|dimensions|nli.enabled|nli.model|rerank.enabled|rerank.model`.
memories.content: `ProviderCache` in `src/ops/mod.rs` keys loaded model bundles by `provider_cache_key = backend|provider|dimensions|nli.enabled|nli.model|rerank.enabled|rerank.model`. Daemon-only and routing-only fields (`idle_timeout_secs`, `socket_path`, `use_for_cli`) deliberately don't affect the key. **If you add a model-affecting config field, extend this key** — the `cache_key_is_deterministic_and_signature_sensitive` test will fail if you forget.

memories.title: Retrieval pipeline
memories.summary: `RetrievalEngine::run` (in `src/retrieval/engine.rs`) is the query pipeline: 1.
memories.content:
`RetrievalEngine::run` (in `src/retrieval/engine.rs`) is the query pipeline:

1. **Filter** — `apply_index_filters` applies hard filters (`types`, `tags`, `min_criticality`, `status`, `include_expired`) at the LanceDB layer.
2. **Vector search** — if a query is present and embeddings are enabled, fetch top-K candidates by vector similarity from LanceDB.
3. **Scope scoring** — for each candidate, compute physical + logical proximity to the query context.
4. **Composite scoring** — `composite_score` blends semantic similarity, scope proximity, criticality × decay, trust weight, and challenge penalty according to which scoring mode is active (`with_query`, `with_keyword`, `scope_only`, `degraded`).
5. **Rerank (optional)** — if `[rerank].enabled`, the top-`top_n` results are re-scored by a cross-encoder model and blended with the original score.
6. **Threshold + truncate** — apply `relevance_threshold` (filter mode only) and `max_results`.

Two modes, `Filter` and `Rank`, gate stage 1's signal requirement: `Filter` requires at least one of `query`/`path`/`logical`/`tags`; `Rank` does not. Downstream stages are identical.

memories.title: Epistemic classes and bi-temporal validity
memories.summary: Every memory carries an **epistemic class** (`Epistemic { Fact, Observation, Decision }`, in `crates/engram-types/src/epistemic.rs`) orthogonal to its `MemoryType`.
memories.content:
Every memory carries an **epistemic class** (`Epistemic { Fact, Observation, Decision }`, in `crates/engram-types/src/epistemic.rs`) orthogonal to its `MemoryType`. The class answers "what kind of claim is this?" — a fact about the world, an observation of behavior at a point in time, or a choice someone made — and it shapes decay anchoring, challenge penalties, situation weighting, and conflict routing.

Two rules keep this backward compatible:

- **Type-derived defaults are frozen.** `MemoryType::default_epistemic()` (context/convention/relationship/hazard → Fact, debug → Observation, decision/intent/preference → Decision) is the compatibility anchor: pre-epistemic files parse to exactly these classes.
- **Off-diagonal-only emission.** The file writer only emits `epistemic:` (and the validity fields) when they differ from the type-derived default. A memory that never uses the new fields round-trips **byte-identical** to its pre-epistemic form — golden tests in `crates/engram-storage/src/memory_file/tests.rs` enforce this.

Validity is **bi-temporal** (`valid_from`, `invalidated_at`, `superseded_by` in the hidden frontmatter): a memory's window can be closed without deleting it. Windows close via supersession (`create`/`update` with `supersedes`), `resolve --action invalidate`, or consolidation (`compress` invalidates its sources). `update --clear-invalidated` reopens a window. Retrieval and `list` exclude closed-window memories by default (`include_invalidated: true` opts back in); GC reaps them only after `invalidated_retention_days`. A **future-dated** `invalidated_at` is still valid until that instant, mirroring `expires_at`.

memories.title: Snapshot tests
memories.summary: CLI output is covered by `insta` snapshots in **two tiers**. Which one a new test belongs in depends on what it is trying to pin down.
memories.content:
CLI output is covered by `insta` snapshots in **two tiers**. Which one a new
test belongs in depends on what it is trying to pin down.

**Tier 1 — the renderers** (`crates/engram-cli/src/output.rs::tests`, snapshots
under `crates/engram-cli/tests/snapshots/renderer/`). Drives every
`OutputFormatter::print_*` method in-process across `pretty`/`json`/`plain`.
Every input is a literal — pinned ids, pinned clocks, no store, no models — so
these snapshots contain the **real rendered bytes with nothing redacted**. Put
anything about *layout* here: it is faster, and a reviewer reads actual output
instead of placeholders.

`OutputFormatter::capturing()` (test-only) swaps the stdout/stderr sinks for
string buffers. Use `snap_formats(case, |f| …)` for the three-format sweep, and
give any new fixture a fixed timestamp via `fixed(…)` — never `Utc::now()`.

**Everything the CLI prints must go through the formatter.** insta does not
read a stream — `assert_snapshot!` compares a `String` — so a bare `println!`
puts its bytes somewhere no in-process test can reach, permanently and
silently. Use `outln!` / `errln!` / `outraw!` / `errraw!`
(`use crate::output::{outln, …};`), which mirror
`println!`/`eprintln!`/`print!`/`eprint!` including the bare `outln!(f)` form.
The `formatter-output` CI job enforces this; it exempts only `output.rs`, which

memories.title: Parallelization and SIMD
memories.summary: A survey of EngramDB's CPU-bound bulk paths, what each one costs, and which ones were worth parallelizing.
memories.content:
A survey of EngramDB's CPU-bound bulk paths, what each one costs, and which
ones were worth parallelizing. Everything here is measured;
`benches/parallel_simd.rs` is the harness and re-running it reproduces the
numbers.

Numbers below: 4-core Intel Xeon @ 2.80GHz (AVX-512 capable), `profile.bench`,
rayon's default pool (4 threads). Treat the ratios as the result, not the
absolute times — `profile.bench` tracks `[profile.release]`'s `opt-level`, and
that value has changed twice over this document's life (`2`, then `"z"`, now
`3`), so an absolute figure only means something next to the profile it was
taken at.

> **How this document evolved.** It started by measuring rayon over the bulk
> paths, then claimed the fast dot product was SIMD, then retracted that after
> disassembly showed it was instruction-level parallelism, then established
> that neither survives the release profile — and arrived at explicit
> intrinsics, which do. Then the release profile itself changed, and the
> intrinsics were deleted. The dead ends are kept because each one is a trap
> someone will otherwise re-enter.

> ## ⚠️ Read this first: the profile changed
>
> **`[profile.release]` is `opt-level = 3`. It was `"z"` for most of this
> document's life, and large parts of it are written against `"z"`.**
>
> Everything below that reasons about `-Oz` — that auto-vectorization is off,
> that portable SIMD crates cannot be used, that hand-written `std::arch`
> intrinsics are the only way to get vector instructions into the binary — was
> true and is now history. It is kept because the measurements are real and the
> reasoning is reusable, not because it describes the build you have.
>
> What is true today:
>
> - `ops::compress::dot_unit` is [`fearless_simd`](https://github.com/linebender/fearless_simd)

memories.title: What the lane trick actually does (a dead end, kept as a warning)
memories.summary: Rust's `f32` addition is IEEE-strict, so a single running sum is a dependency chain the optimizer may not reassociate — each multiply-add waits on the previous one, and the CPU's multiple FP units sit
memories.content:
Rust's `f32` addition is IEEE-strict, so a single running sum is a dependency
chain the optimizer may not reassociate — each multiply-add waits on the
previous one, and the CPU's multiple FP units sit idle. Splitting the
accumulator into eight independent chains removes the dependency:

`chunks_exact` + `try_into` is load-bearing: it hands LLVM a `&[f32; 8]` whose
length is a compile-time constant, so the bounds checks disappear. The same
unrolling written as `&a[k*8..k*8+8]` measured *slower* than the scalar version
(327 ns vs 314 ns) — the slice has a runtime length and the bounds check stays
in the loop. Both variants are kept in the bench as `cosine_f32_lanes8` (slice
indexing, slow) and `cosine_f32_arr8` (array chunks, fast).

**But the eight chains stay scalar.** Disassembling the generated code settles
what LLVM actually emits for `dot_unit`:

So at `opt-level = 2` — which is `profile.bench`, i.e. every benchmark number
in this repo — the eight lanes are eight scalar `xmm` registers issued in
parallel. That is instruction-level parallelism. Only `opt-level = 3` turns
them into packed SSE.

This also re-explains the register-pressure result. `cosine_f32_arr8` computes
three quantities (`Σab`, `Σa²`, `Σb²`), so eight accumulators each means 24
live values against sixteen `xmm` registers — it spills, and lands at 314 ns,
indistinguishable from scalar. One accumulator set fits, and reaches 114 ns:

Getting to one accumulator set is an algorithmic change, not a codegen trick:
L2-normalize each vector once in an O(n) prepass and the O(n²) body is a bare
dot product. That also deletes real work — the old loop recomputed `‖a‖` and
`‖b‖` inside all n(n−1)/2 comparisons even though each vector has exactly one
norm. **Two thirds of the arithmetic was redundant**, and removi

memories.title: The release profile is the whole story
memories.summary: `[profile.release]` sets `opt-level = "z"`, which runs neither the loop vectorizer nor the unroller.
memories.content:
`[profile.release]` sets `opt-level = "z"`, which runs neither the loop
vectorizer nor the unroller. Every arithmetic result in the section above
evaporates there — and the unrolled form is actively *worse* than the naive
loop, because the optimizer that would have cleaned it up is switched off.
Measured at `opt-level = "z"` with the real release profile (`lto = true`,
`codegen-units = 1`), 384-dim pairs:

Two lessons, and the second is the one that matters.

memories.title: Benchmarks lie about this repo
memories.summary: `profile.bench` is `opt-level = 2`; `profile.release` is `opt-level = "z"`.
memories.content:
`profile.bench` is `opt-level = 2`; `profile.release` is `opt-level = "z"`.
**Every Criterion number in this repo is measured on a more aggressively
optimized build than the one users run**, and for arithmetic-bound code the
two profiles do not even rank the candidates the same way. Tuning against
`cargo bench` alone produced a change that was 4.4× faster in the benchmark
and 1.6× *slower* in production. Rayon results are unaffected — thread-level
parallelism does not care about `opt-level` — but anything that depends on
codegen must be checked at `-Oz` before it is believed.

memories.title: Intrinsics work where auto-vectorization cannot
memories.summary: Auto-vectorization is an optimizer pass, so `-Oz` disables it. Intrinsics are *semantic*: `_mm256_fmadd_ps` lowers to `vfmadd231ps` regardless of what the optimizer is doing.
memories.content:
Auto-vectorization is an optimizer pass, so `-Oz` disables it. Intrinsics are
*semantic*: `_mm256_fmadd_ps` lowers to `vfmadd231ps` regardless of what the
optimizer is doing. That makes explicit SIMD the only way to get vector
arithmetic into a size-optimized build — the exact case where hand-written
SIMD earns its keep, and the opposite of the usual advice.

`ops::compress::dot_unit` therefore dispatches: AVX2+FMA when
`is_x86_feature_detected!` says so, SSE2 otherwise (x86-64 baseline, no
detection needed), NEON on aarch64 (mandatory there), single-accumulator
scalar elsewhere. Verified in the actual stripped release binary:
`dot_unit_avx2` contains `vfmadd231ps` and `vaddps`.

**Cost: 2,968 bytes.** 57,717,584 → 57,720,552 (+0.01%).

memories.title: Raising `opt-level` instead — rejected here, adopted later
memories.summary: > **Superseded.** This section rejected raising `opt-level`; the project later > did it anyway.
memories.content:
> **Superseded.** This section rejected raising `opt-level`; the project later
> did it anyway. The measurements stand — the trade really is ~+91% binary for
> ~23% off a reindex — but the conclusion drawn from them was reversed once
> `-Oz` turned out to also be blocking a safe SIMD crate. See
> [Adopting fearless_simd](#adopting-fearless_simd-and-raising-opt-level).

The alternative is to let the auto-vectorizer do it, which means raising
`opt-level` across the whole dependency chain. Both levels were built and
measured end to end (everything else in the profile held fixed; speed is
`reindex --index-only` over a 1,200-memory store, 9 reps, interleaved):

Roughly **double the binary for ~23% off a reindex** — and `3` over `2` buys
~3% more speed for another 5.7 MiB, so `2` is the knee. The binary ships as a
prebuilt artifact (release archives, Homebrew, Scoop) and is spawned per
Claude Code hook invocation, so its size is download and cold-start cost, not
disk.

That is what made this look like a bad trade at the time: the intrinsics got
11–13× on the arithmetic for 3 KB, so the arithmetic did not need `opt-level`.
What the framing missed is that `opt-level` was not only buying arithmetic — it
was also the thing keeping every safe SIMD crate out of the codebase. `2` is
still the knee; it is now the shipped value.

`reindex` improves far less than the microbenchmarks suggest because it is a
*mixed* workload — LanceDB commits, file I/O, allocator traffic — in which
arithmetic-bound code is a small slice.

memories.title: Per-package `opt-level` does not survive fat LTO
memories.summary: The tempting middle ground is to raise `opt-level` for only the hot crates: **This was built, measured, and reverted.** A minimal two-crate reproduction (`hotlib` at `opt-level = 2`, binary at `"z"`,
memories.content:
The tempting middle ground is to raise `opt-level` for only the hot crates:

**This was built, measured, and reverted.** A minimal two-crate reproduction
(`hotlib` at `opt-level = 2`, binary at `"z"`, fat LTO) produces a
**byte-identical binary** — same SHA-256 — to the same build with no override.
`cargo build -v` confirms rustc really is passed `-C opt-level=2`, so the
override is applied and then discarded: the fat-LTO link step re-runs the
pipeline at the top-level profile's `opt-level`. `lto = "thin"` behaves the
same. In the real binary the override changed the size slightly (+1.46%) but
disassembly found no trace of the `opt-level = 2` codegen shape in the hot
function.

Extending it to all seven workspace crates cost **+37.2%** (55.04 → 75.54 MiB)
— LTO inlining monomorphized dependency generics into our crates' codegen
units — for a `reindex` A/B of 196 ms min / 248 ms median baseline vs 192 ms /
201 ms overridden: inside the noise on the minimum.

Reindex would not have moved much regardless: its bulk work is frontmatter
deserialization and Snowball stemming, inside `toml`, `serde_yaml_ng` and
`rust-stemmers`, not in EngramDB's crates.

memories.title: Adopting fearless_simd, and raising `opt-level`
memories.summary: `ops::compress::dot_unit` used to be four hand-written backends (`dot_unit_{sse2,avx2,neon,scalar}`) behind `is_x86_feature_detected!`.
memories.content:
`ops::compress::dot_unit` used to be four hand-written backends
(`dot_unit_{sse2,avx2,neon,scalar}`) behind `is_x86_feature_detected!`. It is
now a single generic kernel over
[`fearless_simd`](https://github.com/linebender/fearless_simd) — and with it
went the last `unsafe` in EngramDB's own logic. (The workspace is not
`unsafe`-free: `engram-onnx` still `dlopen`s the ONNX Runtime, which no crate
can do safely, and two tests call `libc::mkfifo`.)

That was only possible because `[profile.release]` moved off `opt-level = "z"`.
The two decisions are one decision: at `-Oz` the crate was 1.3–2.5× *slower*
than the intrinsics (measured in detail below, and kept, because it is the
reason this took two attempts). At `2` or `3` it is ~1.02× *faster*.

The probe is committed at `tools/simd-probe/` — a standalone crate (its own
`[workspace]`, like `fuzz/`) that mirrors `[profile.release]` key-for-key, with
every candidate timed interleaved in one process. `./size.sh` gives the size
axis. Re-checking a future version is one `cargo run --release`.

memories.title: The numbers that decided it
memories.summary: 384-dim pairs, AVX-512 host, candidates interleaved and scored on their minimum. "intrinsics dispatch" is the old `dot_unit`, verbatim: Three results in that table are worth stating outright.
memories.content:
384-dim pairs, AVX-512 host, candidates interleaved and scored on their
minimum. "intrinsics dispatch" is the old `dot_unit`, verbatim:

Three results in that table are worth stating outright.

**Four accumulators, not two.** Two is the obvious choice — it is what the
hand-written backends did — and it left ~10% on the table. A 512-bit `mul_add`
has enough latency that two dependency chains do not fill the pipeline. Going
to four is the entire difference between 0.90× of the intrinsics and 1.02×. It
cost one line and would never have been found by reasoning about it.

**`opt-level` is the win; the crate is free.** Of the 49.7 → 33.7 ns, almost
all of it (49.7 → 34.4) is the profile change, which the intrinsics would have
got too. fearless_simd's contribution is the last 2% — and deleting four
backends and the `unsafe` in them. Sell it as maintainability that costs
nothing, not as a speedup.

Confirmed in the shipped profile rather than inferred from the benchmark:
the AVX-512 monomorphisation emits `vfmadd231ps` on `zmm` and the AVX2 one
on `ymm`, two accumulators per issue, with `vaddps` folding them at the end.

**The kernel cannot tell `2` from `3`** (33.7 vs 34.3 ns, inside the noise).
That is a fact about the kernel, not about the profile — see
[`2` vs `3`](#2-vs-3-the-kernel-is-the-wrong-place-to-ask) below, where the
*workload* turns out to disagree.

memories.title: The scalar loop never vectorizes, at any `opt-level`
memories.summary: Note row one: 441 ns at `-Oz`, 442 at `2`, 446 at `3`. Raising `opt-level` does **not** make a plain `f32` dot product vectorize, because IEEE addition is not associative and LLVM will not reassociate
memories.content:
Note row one: 441 ns at `-Oz`, 442 at `2`, 446 at `3`. Raising `opt-level` does
**not** make a plain `f32` dot product vectorize, because IEEE addition is not
associative and LLVM will not reassociate the accumulator without fast-math.
That is why this kernel is explicitly SIMD rather than a tidy loop, and it is
unchanged by the profile move. `-Oz` was never the reason explicit SIMD was
needed here; it was only the reason it had to be *unsafe* explicit SIMD.

memories.title: Getting the API right — two mistakes worth not repeating
memories.summary: **The loop shape is `opt-level`-dependent, and reverses.** The crate's documented idiom is zipping two `chunks_exact` iterators (its `sigmoid.rs` example).
memories.content:
**The loop shape is `opt-level`-dependent, and reverses.** The crate's
documented idiom is zipping two `chunks_exact` iterators (its `sigmoid.rs`
example). Hand-rolled `&a[i..i + w]` indexing measured **much better at `-Oz`**
(75 vs 317 ns) and **worse at `2`** (49.8 vs 38.2). Had the API been evaluated
only at `-Oz`, the idiomatic form — the one that wins in production — would
have been discarded as hopeless.

**Do not force a level with `Token::assume_supported()`.** It hands over a
proof token but does *not* enable the target feature on the calling function,
so the body compiles for the baseline and you measure emulation. That route
reported AVX2 ~12× slower than the same kernel through `dispatch!`. The
supported knob is `--cfg disable_dispatch_*` at build time.

memories.title: What v0.7.0 does not have
memories.summary: - **No horizontal sum.** There is no `reduce_sum`, and `SimdSplit` is not among `S::f32s`' trait bounds, so a log-depth lane fold cannot even be *written* generically.
memories.content:
- **No horizontal sum.** There is no `reduce_sum`, and `SimdSplit` is not among
  `S::f32s`' trait bounds, so a log-depth lane fold cannot even be *written*
  generically. Every kernel here ends in a scalar walk over N lanes. It runs
  once per call rather than once per element, so it does not show up at 384
  dims, but it would at 16.
- **No runtime way down a level.** `dispatch!` normalises *up* to the best the
  CPU has (`Level::__dispatch_target`). This has a real testing consequence,
  below.

memories.title: The AVX-512 downgrade: offered, measured, not used
memories.summary: `examples/disable_avx2_for_one_function.rs` exists for the case where "a specific instruction set regresses performance", and downgrading AVX-512 → AVX2 for this kernel looked indicated: at `-Oz` the
memories.content:
`examples/disable_avx2_for_one_function.rs` exists for the case where "a
specific instruction set regresses performance", and downgrading AVX-512 →
AVX2 for this kernel looked indicated: at `-Oz` the AVX-512 level did 32 floats
per iteration for the same time AVX2 took over 16.

It was implemented (`dot_no512` in the probe) and measured: **37.3 ns against
38.2 without it at `opt-level = 2` — inside the noise.** Not shipped.

An earlier revision of this document explained that `-Oz` result as 512-bit
frequency licensing. **That was speculation and it was wrong.** The real cause
is that at `-Oz` the loop is bound by per-element overhead — bounds checks and
an un-inlined wrapper — so vector *width* buys nothing at any level; per float
all three levels cost the same 0.19 ns. Once the optimizer is on and that
overhead is gone, AVX-512 is fine. The lesson is the general one: a mechanism
you did not verify is a guess, and this document should not have stated it as
fact.

memories.title: aarch64: no hardware, but not nothing
memories.summary: The NEON backend was deleted with the rest, and every CI runner and dev box here is x86-64, so "did Apple Silicon regress?" had no obvious way to be answered.
memories.content:
The NEON backend was deleted with the rest, and every CI runner and dev box
here is x86-64, so "did Apple Silicon regress?" had no obvious way to be
answered. Two things can be established off-host, and `./aarch64.sh` in the
probe does both (cross-compile + QEMU + `llvm-mca`; needs `qemu-user-static`,
`gcc-aarch64-linux-gnu`, `llvm`, and the `aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu` target).

**Correctness, exactly.** QEMU user-mode is an architectural emulator — the
arithmetic it performs is the arithmetic the hardware performs. `Level::Neon`
is selected, and the shipped kernel and the deleted NEON backend both agree
with a scalar reference across 23 lengths × 8 seeds, worst absolute error
9.537e-7 against a 1e-5 tolerance.

**Throughput, as a static estimate.** `llvm-mca` models a named core's pipeline
and reports cycles for a loop body; Apple M1 is one of the cores it models. The
two hot loops, extracted from the cross-compiled binary:

Both loops come out at ~4 cycles per iteration on M1 and N1 — but the new one
does 16 floats per iteration against the old one's 8, because four accumulators
fill the pipeline where two left it idle. Same effect as on x86, and it is the
whole margin. On cortex-a72, a narrower older core, the loop is
throughput-bound rather than latency-bound and the advantage mostly disappears.

Worth noting separately: at `opt-level = 3` the kernel **inlines** on aarch64 —
four `fmla` sit directly in `dot_fearless` with no `bl vectorize_neon`. At
`-Oz` it did not, and that out-of-line wrapper was the single biggest reason
the crate lost there. The disassembly is the evidence that the profile change
fixed it on ARM too, not only on x86.

**What this is not: a wall-clock benchmark.** QEMU timings are meaningless (it
translates to x86), and `llvm-mca` assumes a perfe

memories.title: Per-level test coverage had to be rebuilt
memories.summary: The hand-written backends could be called directly, so one test run checked SSE2, AVX2, NEON and scalar together.
memories.content:
The hand-written backends could be called directly, so one test run checked
SSE2, AVX2, NEON and scalar together. `dispatch!` offers no runtime way down,
and every dev box and CI runner has AVX2 or better — so the SSE2 kernel, which
is what every pre-Haswell CPU and every AVX2-masking VM executes, would have
been compiled, shipped, and never once executed.

The `simd-levels` CI job restores the guarantee by rebuilding the arithmetic
tests under each `--cfg disable_dispatch_*` combination. **This is not
optional bookkeeping** — it is the only thing standing between a green suite
and an untested kernel on the CPUs least likely to be in front of a developer.

memories.title: `2` vs `3`: the kernel is the wrong place to ask
memories.summary: The dot product cannot distinguish them — 33.7 ns at `2` against 34.3 at `3`, inside the run-to-run spread.
memories.content:
The dot product cannot distinguish them — 33.7 ns at `2` against 34.3 at `3`,
inside the run-to-run spread. On that evidence `2` was chosen, and an earlier
revision of this document justified it with a borrowed figure: that `3` bought
"~3% more speed for another 5.7 MiB".

**Both halves of that were wrong**, and the whole-program measurement is what
showed it. Three binaries, one commit, one machine, `reindex --index-only` over
a 1,200-memory store, interleaved round-robin and scored on the minimum of 15:

`3` over `2` is **~5% faster for ~4.7% more binary** — close to 1:1, and an
easy call once the +82% step has been taken. The old claim had it as 3% for
5.7 MiB, i.e. a clearly bad trade.

The reason the microbenchmark misleads is worth internalising, because it is
the same shape as the `-Oz` mistake earlier in this document: **`reindex` is
not arithmetic-bound.** Its time goes to TOML frontmatter deserialization and
Snowball stemming, and those are exactly the code `3` helps and the dot product
is not. Tuning the profile on the kernel measures the one part of the workload
that had already been hand-optimised into insensitivity.

This also retired the `[profile.release.package.*]` block. Fourteen crates were
pinned to `opt-level = 3` back when the profile was `"z"`; with the profile at
`3` every entry named the value it already had.

shifting inlining decisions, since a per-package profile feeds c

memories.title: Size — what this actually cost
memories.summary: Two scales. The kernel itself is noise; the profile change is the bill.
memories.content:
Two scales. The kernel itself is noise; the profile change is the bill.

**The kernel.** `.text` bytes added over a plain scalar loop, from `size.sh`
(differencing three minimal single-kernel binaries so std and formatting
cancel; the fearless case carries the same four-accumulator body that ships):

fearless_simd is never the smaller option — `dispatch!` emits a copy of the
kernel per SIMD level where the hand-written code emitted two — and four
accumulators cost ~900 bytes over two. At ~4 KB more than the intrinsics on a
100 MB binary this does not register.

**The profile.** This is the real number, and it is large. Same commit range,
same machine, same toolchain, both `cargo build --release`:

The binary ships as a prebuilt artifact (release archives, Homebrew, Scoop) and
is spawned per Claude Code hook invocation, so this is download and cold-start
cost, not disk. It was accepted deliberately.

Note the earlier section quotes a `-Oz` baseline of 57,717,584 bytes. That
